en: The Great Treasure Extensive Pavilion Well-Abiding Secret Dhāraṇī Sūtra,
Volume One.
Grand Master of the Household, Peer of the State, Special Advancement, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Daxingshan Monastery, who was the Duke of Sū, with a fief of three thousand households, invested with the purple robe, posthumously honored as Minister of Works, and titled Dajian (Great Mirror), under imperial decree. Chapter One: The Introduction Thus have I heard.
At one time, the Bhagavān was dwelling in the great city of Rājagṛha.
During his first assembly, he subdued the māra-armies numbering in the koṭis and tamed all the non-Buddhist extremists.
Having abandoned birth and death and crossed over all the torrents,
at that time, hundreds of thousands of nayutas of *kṛṅgara* and *bimbara* māra armies pervaded Jambudvīpa.
At that time, by the Buddha’s supernatural power,
the World-Honored One transformed this great earth so that it became entirely composed of vajra,
ensuring that the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa would not hear even the word "fear."
At that time, the various weapons rained down by Māra’s army were all transformed into flowers.
In the crossroads of Rājagṛha,
great lotuses spontaneously surged forth from the earth.
The flower has a thousand petals and is adorned with the seven treasures;
its pedestal is made of gold and its stem of lapis lazuli, reaching as high as the Brahma-heaven.
It emits various kinds of radiance that pervade the ten directions.
From within those flowers, a voice spontaneously issued forth,
reciting a dhāraṇī named "Awakening.
The dhāraṇī is as follows:
Namo sarvatathāgatebhyo viyūhite tiṣṭhanidhanāśaniḥ | Oṃ maṇivajre hṛdayavajre marāse nyavi-dra-paṇi ||
Hana hana vajra-jaṃbhe traṃ tre saṃmāravānī hūṃ hūṃ saṃdhara saṃdhara buddha-maitri sarva-tathāgata...
*Vajrakalpadhiṣṭhite svāhā.* When this dhāraṇī had thus flowed forth from within that lotus, [the Buddha said: "Svāhā."
Furthermore, a wondrous sound issued forth, pervading the trichiliocosm, praising:
"Excellent, Śākyamuni Tathāgata!
You have already crossed the great ocean of birth and death and utterly annihilated the armies of Māra."
Having departed from the dust of afflictions and shattered the shell of ignorance,
one kindles the great torch of the Dharma. By the majestic power of this dhāraṇī,
it causes the great earth to be transformed into vajra.
Having subdued the hosts of Māra,
at that time the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, Lord of Secrets,
was filled with joy and exultation, and the hairs on his body stood on end.
Prostrating at the Buddha’s feet, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, from which assembly of Buddhas was this dhāraṇī first obtained?
Since ancient times, I have never heard of or seen it among any in the world.”
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, Lord of Secrets:
"There is a dhāraṇī named 'The Great Maṇi Vast Pavilion, the Secret of Excellent Abiding.'"
By the majestic power of this dhāraṇī,
it is able to transform the trichiliocosm into vajra,
and cause all the weapons of the māra armies to be transformed into flowers.
By the majestic spiritual power of this dhāraṇī,
he subdues all hosts of Māras and transforms all other classes of sentient beings, causing them all to be tamed.
By the majestic spiritual power of this dhāraṇī.
A lotus flower surged forth at the crossroads,
and he spoke again to Vajrapāṇi, saying:
"If I were not to rely on this dhāraṇī..."
They cannot achieve equal and perfect enlightenment;
they cannot subdue the hosts of Māra, however many there may be;
and they cannot dry up the great ocean of afflictions.
One cannot kindle the great torch of the Dharma.
Vajrapāṇi, throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of kalpas,
although I have practiced difficult austerities, I have still been unable to accomplish the fruit of Bodhi.
By merely hearing this great dhāraṇī and practicing it in accordance with its application,
one attains perfect awakening.
Vajrapāṇi, this is that dhāraṇī.
It possesses great power and great excellence;
it is the true dharmatā of all Tathāgatas,
which causes all Tathāgatas to perfectly realize the Dharmakāya.
Vajrapāṇi, by reciting the name of this dhāraṇī,
one has already recited the names of all the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas of the ten directions;
if one can merely bring it to mind, [the merit is attained].

This constitutes the worship and offering to all Tathāgatas. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi, with various flowers, various incenses, ointments, and powdered perfumes, [made offerings].
Having made offerings to the Buddha,
and having completed three circumambulations to the right, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One, this dhāraṇī..."
It possesses great majesty and great excellence.
We pray that the World-Honored One will explain for the sake of all sentient beings what kind of extraordinary merits manifest in that world.
No sentient being can hear this dhāraṇī through meager roots of goodness;
this dhāraṇī is equal to the body of the Tathāgata.
The *dharmatā* of the śarīra is the same.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, saying:
"Vajrapāṇi, sentient beings are inferior and do not apply themselves with diligent vigor."
Their minds are greatly deluded and confused, ignorant, dull-witted,
and addicted to various sensual desires; they lack faith in the True Dharma,
and they show no respect for their parents, nor for śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas.
Because they do not respect the Venerable One,
this dhāraṇī does not enter the hands of such persons;
they possess little merit, little wisdom, and little insight.
Such sentient beings are unable to hear it,
unable to uphold it, and do not give rise to pure faith;
yet this dhāraṇī can extinguish all sins.
This is the secret treasury of all the Tathāgatas.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, saying:
"O son of good family, I shall now speak it for you."
To the east of this world, passing through as many *koṭī-nayuta* Buddha-worlds as there are sands in immeasurable Ganges Rivers,
there is a world named Ratnapradīpa, which is composed of the seven precious jewels.
The city was one yojana in width on all four sides.
It was filled with many people living in peace, security, abundance, and joy.
There were men and women, as well as boys and girls.
His body was adorned with all manner of necklaces and ornaments;
a most exquisite jewel crown embellished his head;
his countenance was dignified and majestic, and he possessed great power and majesty.
He was courageous, vigorous, diligent, and fully endowed with wisdom;
he had mastered all arts.
In that city there was a king named Ratnottama.
He was surrounded by eighty koṭis of ministers who served as his assistants.
The king’s queen was named Prabhāratna (Jewel of Light),
and he had twenty thousand palace ladies.
All were like celestial maidens attending them from before and behind.
The flower trees and various incense trees produced within that world were all composed of the seven treasures.
The various flowers growing in water are also composed of the seven treasures;
all the flowers growing on land are made of Jāmbūnada gold.
The lifespan of the people in that land is eighty thousand kalpas.
They all accomplished the ten paths of wholesome action and gave rise to great pure faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
That king nourished and protected them through the True Dharma, not through what is contrary to the Dharma.
He constantly brings benefit to all sentient beings.
In that world, there is a Buddha named Endowed with Various Purely Adorned Mani Jewels, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
In that world, he will attain buddhahood and extensively perform the deeds of a Buddha,
with a retinue consisting of a great multitude of immeasurable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and a host of great vidyādhara sages known as the "All-Knowing."
That Tathāgata’s body is the color of purple-gold;
he is endowed with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs of excellence,
and his halo extends one fathom.
Its light pervaded everywhere,
like the blazing radiance of the seven precious jewels;
the bodies of all the bodhisattvas were entirely golden, shimmering with the marks and signs of excellence.
Seated with majestic dignity upon lotus flowers made of the seven precious gems,
they all possess unimpeded eloquence and have thoroughly mastered the fields of knowledge;
together, they contemplate the Great Jewel Maṇi Vast Pavilion Secret Dharāṇī.
By the majestic spiritual power of this dhāraṇī,
such supreme merits are produced. That Buddha,
the World-Honored One, for the sake of all sentient beings...
I shall expound this dharani method.
By hearing this dharani, those sentient beings will constantly obtain peace and happiness.
All those sentient beings were freed from the realms of hell, the animal kingdom, the world of Yama,
and the bodies of asuras;
all gates to the evil destinies were completely closed.
He opens the gates to all the heavens and opens the gates to all the happy realms.
All sentient beings in that world abide entirely in unsurpassed bodhi;
all those sentient beings dwell with minds of loving-kindness, like water and milk blended together.
In the distant past, when that Buddha, the World-Honored One, was practicing the bodhisattva path,
he cultivated this dharani method and made this vow:
"May all sentient beings who are born in my buddha-field..."
They are all certain not to regress from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
If there are sentient beings who hear this dhāraṇī,
receive and uphold it, read and recite it, and practice it with diligent application.
One should maintain mindfulness without abandoning it to seek great accomplishment,
until one hears its name, or touches it with the hand,
or wears it upon the body, or even merely beholds it with the eyes.
Whether written on scrolls, inscribed upon silk or plain cloth,
or painted upon walls—
whosoever among all sentient beings should behold them.
Those who have committed the five heinous crimes or the four grave offenses; those who slander the true Dharma or the noble ones;
hunters, butchers, executioners, and *naṃba* (butchers).
They spread out their robes:
the blind, the deaf, the sightless, the hunchbacked—
those loathed by others— the mute, and the lepers.
Those who are impoverished and lowly, those of indeterminate karma,
those bound by the net of Māra, those fallen into wrong views,
those afflicted by Vināyakas, and those oppressed by malevolent stars.
As for those harmed by the seven luminaries, upon hearing this dhāraṇī,
they shall certainly realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Even down to animals— deer, birds, mosquitoes, gadflies, moths, ants,
and other such beings born from eggs, from wombs, by transformation, or from moisture—
whoever hears the name of this dhāraṇī.
"You shall certainly realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
you should not harbor any doubt.
When the World-Honored One had spoken these words, at that time—
The entire great assembly was filled with immense joy;
the hairs on their bodies stood erect.
At that time, the heavens rained down *pāṭala* flowers and *puṇḍarīka* flowers.
Mandārava flowers and mahāmandārava flowers [fell].
In the void of space, various kinds of subtle and exquisite celestial music played spontaneously without being struck.
At that time, the great assembly in the gathering...
Each and every one saw their own bodies radiating light.
Before the Tathāgata, there spontaneously emerged a seven-jeweled pavilion,
magnificent and beautiful, a sight that all people delighted to behold.
The four pillars, four gates, and four stairways of that precious pavilion were brilliantly illuminated.
At the four corners of the pavilion stood four great jewels, blazing like the sun.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable mani-jewels strung upon the netting,
with countless jeweled bells suspended above it,
and adorned with immeasurable silk banners.
Various exquisite flowers hung down in an intermingled array.
At that time, the great earth shook in six ways,
manifesting the signs of trembling, quaking, roaring, surging, subsiding, and heaving.
The light from the celestial palaces of the various devas shines upon and touches [them],
and wherever that light reaches, all are awakened.
The same is true for the Four Great Heavenly Kings, the Vidyādharas, and others.
All the palaces of Māra blazed with rising flames;
all obstructors and Vināyakas were utterly terrified,
fleeing in the ten directions while wailing aloud.
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted a great radiance from the tuft of hair between his eyebrows.
This light shone universally, awakening all Buddhas within all Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions.
Once they had been awakened, the light withdrew once more and entered the crown of the Buddha’s head.
Then, all the Buddhas of the ten directions raised their voices in unison to praise the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, saying:
Excellent, excellent, Śākyamuni Tathāgata!
You should now proceed to the world-system called Jewel Lamp, to the presence of the Tathāgata Adorned with Various Purely Established Endowed Maṇis.
May this great assembly be permitted to follow along to behold, pay homage to, and make offerings to [the Buddha],
and may they also extensively hear the Dharma of the Great Jewel Vast Pavilion Well-Abiding Secret Dhāraṇī.
Why is this? Because this dhāraṇī possesses great majesty and power;
it has been collectively empowered by all the Tathāgatas of the past.
If there should be anyone who hears this dhāraṇī, [they shall attain such benefits].
Even those who merely hear its name or touch it with their hands will certainly attain the stage of non-retrogression and realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
At that time, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, having heard the requests from all the Tathāgatas throughout the worlds of the ten directions, [responded].
He further emitted immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of rays of light and addressed the assembly, saying:
"I now wish to go to the world-system of Jewel Lamp."
"The time has now arrived;
you all should quickly prepare yourselves to follow me.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata rose from his seat.
He approached the seven-jeweled pavilion and touched it with his hand;
from within that pavilion, a magnificent lion throne made of vajra suddenly emerged.
That throne was composed of the seven precious substances and was most exquisitely adorned.
Those who saw him were delighted.
Furthermore, a wondrous lotus flower appeared upon his seat,
composed of the seven precious gems, with a stem of gold and a pericarp of ruby.
At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, spread his seat upon a lotus flower and sat down.
Then the entire world shook with a great trembling.
The Tathāgata immediately entered the Great Jewel Pure Samādhi and, by the power of this samādhi, brought peace and comfort to the entire assembly.
He proceeded to the void,
together with the entire assembly and their retinues,
as well as the retinues of the great Bodhisattvas, and the great devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans.
The immeasurable hosts of vidyādhara sages, together with Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Secrets,
and all the Śakras, Brahmās, Lokapālas, and the four Great Kings,
ascended into the void and proceeded toward the eastern direction.
Passing through countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddha-fields, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
he reached the World of Jewel Lamps in a single kṣaṇa.
Descending from the sky, he went to the presence of the Tathāgata Adorned with Various Pure Maṇi Jewels.
He respectfully inquired after his health, asking whether he had little affliction, was free from distress,
and was light and well in his daily activities. At that time,
the Tathāgata Śākyamuni took a thousand-petaled lotus flower composed of the seven precious gems.
He offered it to that Buddha.
At that time, the Tathāgata was in a magnificent celestial palace within a great assembly,
and extending his golden arm, he comforted Śākyamuni, the Arhat Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Having offered consolation, he sat within a jeweled pavilion and addressed the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, saying:
"Bhagavān, you have already turned the Great Wheel of Dharma and subdued the armies of Māra."
He has kindled the great torch of the Dharma, erected the banner of the Dharma,
struck the great drum of the Dharma, and blown the great conch of the Dharma;
having performed the Buddha-work in that world, he has realized the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*).
"Bhagavān, you shall now further turn the second wheel of Dharma;
you shall open the treasury of the True Dharma within Jambudvīpa.
As soon as these words were spoken, those buddha-fields shook in eighteen ways.
That which is called "moving" reaches the ultimate in moving and moves everywhere;
"shaking" reaches the ultimate in shaking and shakes everywhere;
"vibrating" reaches the ultimate in vibrating and vibrates everywhere, roaring.
Utterly roaring and roaring everywhere;
striking intensely and striking everywhere;
surging intensely and surging everywhere.
At that time, the heavens rained down exquisite flowers as a great spiritual miracle manifested.
In the midst of the void, various kinds of music played spontaneously without being struck, their sounds pleasing to the mind.
Furthermore, the sons of the gods played various kinds of music.
All the devas and nāgas rained down various jewels, various incenses, various sandalwood perfumed waters, various garments, and various ornaments.
They rained down exquisite red pearls, agates, and the great jewels of Vairocana— the sun-treasures and moon-lovers.
They rained down the auspicious-treasury great maṇi-jewels and exquisite celestial blue lotuses.
Kumuda lotuses and puṇḍarīka lotuses rained down,
as did māndārava flowers and mahāmāndārava flowers,
and celestial, exquisite jāmbūnada gold flowers.
They rained down exquisite silver flowers and exquisite pearls;
the sons of the gods, from within the void of space,
produced subtle and wondrous sounds, joyfully offering praise.
Their voices echoed and resounded one after another:
"Excellent, excellent, Śākyamuni Tathāgata!
At this very moment, you are once again turning the wheel of Dharma."
In Jambudvīpa, he erected the great, wondrous, jewel-like Dharma banner of the wish-fulfilling gem,
namely, the Great Teaching of the Secret Dhāraṇī of the Vast and Spacious Pavilion of the Great Jewel, the Well-Established.
O King, it is now being widely disseminated throughout Jambudvīpa.
At that time, the various pure and exquisite maṇi-jewels established the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
From the tuft of hair between his eyebrows, light radiated forth;
that light universally illumined the Buddha-fields of the ten directions and awakened all Tathāgatas.
That light further illuminated the trichiliocosm, as well as all the celestial palaces, all the dragon palaces, all the hells, the animal realm, the realm of Yama, and the hosts of asuras.
Having universally illuminated and awakened all beings,
that light withdrew again and circled three times to the right around that Buddha and the Tathāgata Śākyamuni.
It then vanished into the crown of his head.
At that time, all the Buddhas of the worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Ganges Rivers,
each performed great supernatural transformations in their respective native lands.
Having manifested these supernatural transformations, they proceeded to that world.
Each, by means of their great supernormal powers, emanated a pavilion made of the seven treasures.
Within each pavilion, there appeared a lion throne of pure Jāmbūnada gold.
All those Buddhas together with their retinues sat within the pavilions.
At that time, the Tathāgata was established by various pure, exquisite, and majestic maṇi-jewels, which provided him with consolation.
All those Tathāgatas performed a great offering through their great supernormal powers;
having thus made offerings to those Buddhas, they [proceeded].
He returned and sat upon the lion throne.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maṇigarbha went to the presence of the Tathāgata Endowed with Various Purely Adorned Maṇis.
Prostrating with his head at the Buddha’s feet, he addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, there now appears this great assembly of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, as well as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and the great assembly of vidyādhara sages."
With the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi as their leader,
these great mahāsattvas have manifested great supernormal transformations.
We pray that you will proclaim the Great Jewel Vast Pavilion Well-Established Secret Dhāraṇī.
"Now is precisely the right time.
Thus he requested a second and a third time.
At that moment, the Tathāgata was established by the various pure and exquisite mani-jewels of Endaraṇa.
He addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maṇigarbha, saying:
"Go to the presence of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni and request [teachings] from that Buddha."
"I shall explain it for you.
Then, the Bodhisattva Maṇigarbha went to where the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, was staying.
Having circumambulated the Buddha three times, he joined his palms in prostration, stood before him,
and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One,
I now entreat the World-Honored One to expound the Great Jewel Vast Pavilion Well-Abiding Secret Dhāraṇī."
Out of compassion and for the benefit of all sentient beings,
at that time the Tathāgata Śākyamuni,
having accepted the request of the Bodhisattva Maṇigarbha, [proceeded].
He then addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Secrets, saying:
"Lord of Secrets, go before the great assembly and strike the ground with your vajra."
Then the Lord of Secrets, Vajrapāṇi,
receiving the holy command of the Buddha,
struck the earth with his vajra within the assembly hall.
As soon as he struck the ground, the earth split apart in four directions.
At that moment, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways,
and from the fissures, pavilions made of the seven precious jewels surged forth.
The four corners, four pillars, and four gates of that pavilion were magnificent and extraordinary,
with all marks and features perfectly complete;
it was resplendent with light and possessed four stairways.
It is three yojanas in height and five yojanas in length and breadth,
being perfectly symmetrical. Within the pavilion appears a stūpa of Jāmbūnada gold,
adorned with various kinds of precious jewels.
A canopy of nets made of the seven treasures covers its top;
immeasurable jeweled bells hang from its four corners,
interspersed with exquisite flowers and silken streamers.
Within that stūpa are the bodies of three Tathāgatas.
At that time, all the Tathāgatas together with the great assembly of Bodhisattvas collectively made offerings to the three Tathāgatas within the jeweled pavilion stūpa.
That is to say: with flower garlands, incense for burning, unguents, powdered incense, banners, flags, and precious canopies;
playing various kinds of music and joining their palms in reverent salutation—at that time, the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth.
The entire assembly gazed upon him with full attention;
all conceived a sense of wonder and rarity,
and they all spoke these words:
From where did this precious pavilion and stūpa come?
Uttering loud cries of praise, they exclaimed, "How marvelous! How rare!
They circumambulated it while singing hymns and offering floral incense, powdered incense, and ointment incense, along with various musical instruments.
He made offerings to the stūpa of the Jewel Pavilion,
joined his palms in prostration, and stood gazing up at it.
At that time, a voice issued forth from within the pavilion, saying:
"You great assembly, you may observe the sky.
Having heard these words, the entire assembly looked toward the sky and immediately beheld vast cloud-leaves composed of great vaidūrya jewels suspended in the void.
Upon those precious cloud-leaves,
this Great Jewel Vast Pavilion Well-Established Secret Dhāraṇī was inscribed in gold. Then,
from the expanse of space, a voice resounded, saying:
"You all, the Buddhas and the great assembly of Bodhisattvas,
should all recite this *dhāraṇī* upon the leaves of the Jewel Cloud.
Having uttered these words, [the sound emerged].
Before each of the Buddhas who have come from the ten directions,
there appeared cloud-leaves made of vaidūrya jewel,
upon each of which this dhāraṇī was inscribed in gold.
Again, this sound was uttered:
"Homage to the Tathāgata Śākyamuni!
May you now open the gate of this precious gabled stūpa."
Within that stūpa,
there are the bodies of three Tathāgatas;
it is by virtue of the majestic spiritual power of these three Tathāgatas that [this occurs].
Manifesting great supernormal transformations of sublime appearance,
those three Tathāgatas shall fully expound this Great Jewel Vast Pavilion Well-Abiding Secret Dhāraṇī within this assembly.
Together with the vidyā-mantras for the accomplishment of the maṇḍala,
at that time all the Buddhas who had come from the ten directions spoke these words:
"We pray only that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni [will grant this]."
For the sake of the great assembly, he opened this stūpa door,
enabling the entire congregation to behold the three Tathāgatas,
namely, the Tathāgata Maṇiratnakusumadhvajarāja.
The Tathāgata Citramaṇi, the Tathāgata,
Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vajrottaraspharaṇarāja—
at that time, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni manifested great supernormal powers.
He proceeded to the Ratnakoṭi Stūpa,
extended his golden arm adorned with the hundred merits,
and opened the door of the stūpa.
He manifested the bodies of three Tathāgatas.
Then the three Tathāgatas praised Śākyamuni, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, Śākyamuni Tathāgata!"
"Now, the Wheel of Dharma is being turned once again in Jambudvīpa;
may the Bhagavān sit here.
At that time, Śākyamuni Tathāgata—
He immediately ascended the jeweled stūpa and sat upon the same seat as the three Tathāgatas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi prostrated himself before the Tathāgata Śākyamuni.
He addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One,
from where have these three Tathāgatas now come to this pavilion and the stūpa?
The Buddha said, "In the distant past, inconceivable, immeasurable, incomparable, and beyond countless kalpas ago..."
In this Jambudvīpa,
the multitude of people shall be secure, prosperous, and happy;
fragrant rice will ripen naturally without being sown.
At that time, there were no people with notions of self or other, nor was there any accumulation of property.
Furthermore, no Buddha had appeared in the world.
There was, however, a king of jewel mountains.
Within that king of mountains dwell three sages:
the first is named Ratnaśikhin,
and the second is named Suvarṇaśikhin.
The three were named Vajraśikhins.
Those three sages reflected with certainty upon the Triple Gem— the Buddha, the Dharma,
and the Saṅgha— and further thought:
"When shall we attain Buddhahood,
realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, and deliver all sentient beings?
Having thus reflected, those sages and others thought as follows.

After remaining silent for a moment, because he again gave rise to his former thought, he immediately realized the *samādhi* of various palatial towers characterized by loving-kindness and joy toward all sentient beings.
He then obtained the divine eye and, looking upward, saw the Śuddhāvāsa deities; furthermore, a voice resounded in the sky, saying:
Excellent, excellent, O noble son, that you are able to give rise to such a supreme mind—
namely, the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Have you not heard of the Great Jewel Vast Pavilion Well-Abiding Secret Dhāraṇī?
All Tathāgatas of the past have already expounded this for the benefit of all sentient beings;
as soon as one hears this dhāraṇī, [the benefits are attained].
One shall attain non-retrogression from unsurpassed bodhi;
all Buddha-dharmas shall manifest before one;
and one shall realize all samādhis.
All dhāraṇī methods will manifest before them;
they will be well able to subdue all demonic armies and kindle the great torch of the Dharma.
All roots of goodness shall manifest before them;
they shall fulfill the six pāramitās and be able to liberate all beings from the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, the world of Yama, and the asuras.
And from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction,
they shall forever attain liberation.
This shall come to pass in future ages.
In this Jambudvīpa, sentient beings are unfilial toward their parents;
they do not revere śramaṇas or brahmins,
nor do they respect their elders.
To slander the True Dharma and revile the Sages,
one should fall into hell;
to slander the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, kill Arhats, and commit the five crimes of immediate retribution.
Those who kill brahmins and those who kill cows;
those who plunder, rob, steal, and speak falsely; those who take what is not given;
and those who engage in sexual misconduct and cause the separation of those who are in harmony.
Those who speak words of defilement, those who use light scales and small measures,
those who forcibly seize property, those who conceal the wealth of others,
those who speak falsely and betray their trust, and those who are driven by the evil karma of previous lives.
All those classes of sentient beings,
by the power of this dhāraṇī, whether reading it,
reciting it, or upholding it, [shall attain...]
Whether worn upon the body, written within clothing,
placed atop a banner,
inscribed upon a scroll, or written upon silk, cotton cloth, walls, or wooden plaques.
Even those who merely hear the sound, touch it with their hands, or see its shadow,
as well as those who subsequently touch others [who have been so affected],
will certainly attain non-retrogressive, unsurpassed enlightenment.
In this present life, one shall obtain immeasurable hundreds of thousands of merits;
remaining far removed from all transgressions, one shall accomplish all roots of goodness, subdue all māras,
and be held in reverence and affection by all in the world.
In all places, they shall receive offerings;
all kings, princes, ministers, and those in the inner palace,
along with their retinues, shall all be filled with joy.
All śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas likewise rejoiced;
his voice was majestic and solemn, a delight for all to hear;
his hands and feet were supple, and the tone of his speech was harmonious and elegant.
They will be free from poverty and shall not suffer the calamities of the world, such as poisons, weapons, swords, water, or fire.
They will not be harmed by the fear of wild beasts,
nor will they have fear of bandits or fear of robbery and plunder.
There is no fear of caṇḍālas, nor fear of nāmas;
whether traveling on great or small paths, there is no fear at all.
There is no fear of yakṣas, nor fear of rākṣasas or piśācas.
There shall be no fear of *nāginīs* and no fear of venomous snakes;
furthermore, for one, two, three, or four days, all forms of malaria—
whether intermittent, chronic, or otherwise— shall not afflict the body.
Diseases of the eyes, diseases of the ears, diseases of the nose, diseases of the tongue;
diseases of the teeth, diseases of the lips, diseases of the throat, diseases of the neck;
diseases of the various limbs, diseases of the hands, diseases of the back, diseases of the waist, diseases of the navel, hemorrhoids, and urinary disorders.
Dysentery, fistula sores, diseases of the thighs, and pain in the calves and feet;
carbuncles, swellings, scrofula, and eruptive rashes;
abdominal pain, scabies, blisters, lameness, leprosy, and ringworm.
They shall be free from such illnesses;
they shall suffer no headaches, nor be blind, nor squint, nor be hunchbacked;
and they shall not meet with untimely or accidental death.
One shall not be deaf or mute, nor shall one be subjected to contempt or deception;
such things as these will not be experienced in the present life.
One shall attain unimpeded eloquence, and at the time of death, the mind shall remain undisturbed.
All Buddhas appear before them to offer consolation;
they shall not be afflicted by sorcery, malevolent spells, or curses.
Whether lying down or awake, their bodies shall be at peace.
Within that dream, one sees hundreds of thousands of buddha-fields,
as well as various buddhas surrounded by bodhisattvas;
this is due to the power of this secret dhāraṇī.
Having attained such supreme merit, that rishi,
filled with the joy of realizing the Dharma, felt his heart leap with exultation;
he then relinquished his life at that very dwelling place.
The body he had relinquished was like fresh butter that dissolves and merges into the earth;
at the very spot where it vanished, three bamboos sprang forth,
with golden stalks and leaves and roots made of the seven precious gems.
Upon every branch and twig there are pearls;
their fragrance is rich and pervasive, and they are constantly radiant.
All who behold them are without exception filled with joy.
When these bamboos have grown for ten months, they spontaneously split open.
Within each bamboo, a young boy is born,
with features so upright and handsome that all who see him find joy.
Possessing the most supreme majesty and a complexion of exquisite beauty, they were endowed with all the marks of excellence.
At that time, the three youths sat cross-legged beneath the bamboo on that very spot and immediately entered right concentration.
On the seventh day, at the middle of the night, they all attained perfect enlightenment.

Their bodies were golden in color, adorned with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics, and graced by a halo of light; at that time, those three bamboo stalks all transformed into pavilions made of the seven treasures.
Furthermore, in the midst of space, the Great Jewel Vast and Expansive Pavilion, the Secret Dhāraṇī of Good Abiding,
suddenly appeared with characters formed of gold.
At that time, there were the Four Great Heavenly Kings.
These are the celestial king Ratnaśikhin, the lord of nāgas;
the celestial king Ratnagarbha, the lord of kumbhāṇḍas; the celestial king Vicitraprabhamahoraga, the lord of mahoragas;
and the celestial king Maṇivajra, the lord of yakṣas.
Each held a precious parasol to cover him from above and proclaimed the Buddha’s merits.
These four heavenly kings each had immeasurable hundreds of thousands of attendants.
They all took exquisite flowers as offerings and spoke these words:
"Now the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has appeared in the world."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi, saying:
"Were those three sages of old anyone else?
They are none other than these three Tathāgatas within this jeweled pavilion stūpa."
The three bamboos of that time are this present magnificent pavilion;
the earth of that time is this present earth;
and the world of that time is this present world.
Because those three rishis diligently practiced this dhāraṇī upon hearing it,
they cast off their bodies as rishis and attained perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, Vajrapāṇi, at that time in the sky...
As for this Devaputra of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven who praised this dhāraṇī, could he be anyone else? It was none other than myself.
Furthermore, there was an attendant named Śuddhāvāsa.
He constantly and diligently served those three sages;
once those three sages had attained perfect enlightenment, he likewise made offerings to them.
For their sake, he received a prophecy from the Śuddhāvāsa deities, saying:
"In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood.
Could the one from the Pure Abodes be anyone else?
It is this very Tathāgata, Endowed with Dignity, Adorned with Various Pure Maṇis, who has now been established."
At that time, all the Buddhas who had come from the worlds of the ten directions unanimously praised the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! You are able to employ the supernatural empowerment of a Tathāgata."
He spoke of this past causal connection to manifest the secret dhāraṇī of the Tathāgata;
this dhāraṇī is the secret of all Tathāgatas.
This is the mother of all Tathāgatas;
it is the secret dhāraṇī that is the heart of all Tathāgatas;
it is the secret dhāraṇī by which all Tathāgatas turn the wheel of Dharma.
This is the secret dhāraṇī of all Tathāgatas for proceeding to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
This is the secret dhāraṇī of all Tathāgatas for approaching the Vajra-Lion Throne.
This is the secret dhāraṇī of the miraculous play of the supernatural powers of all Tathāgatas.
This is the secret dhāraṇī of the perfection of the pāramitās of all Tathāgatas.
This is the secret dhāraṇī of empowerment through the Prajñāpāramitā of all Tathāgatas;
this is the secret mantra-dhāraṇī of all Tathāgatas.
This is the secret dhāraṇī of the maṇḍala of all Tathāgatas;
this is the secret dhāraṇī of the firm-holding mudrā of all Tathāgatas;
this is the secret dhāraṇī of the emission of light by *kūṭāgāras* of all Tathāgatas.
This is the secret dhāraṇī of the ultimate reality of all Tathāgatas;
this is the secret dhāraṇī of the miraculous empowerment of the samādhis of all Tathāgatas.
This is the secret dhāraṇī that adorns the bodhicitta of all bodhisattvas;
this is the secret dhāraṇī that establishes all bodhisattvas in the stage of the Tathāgata.
"This is the secret dhāraṇī for penetrating all samādhis;
this is the secret dhāraṇī for crushing all obstacles.
Are you now reciting it?"
At that time, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha,
abiding in right mindfulness and wisdom, observed all the Tathāgatas and emitted the great Brahma-sound.
He further radiated hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of various kinds of light.
That which is called blue, yellow, red, white,
and purple pervades the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions;
having shone forth, it illuminates them all.
It alerted all the Tathāgatas.
The light then withdrew and circled the Buddha three times before vanishing into the crown of the Buddha's head.
Once it had vanished, [the Buddha said:]
At that time, the World-Honored One, with a pure and wondrous Brahma-voice, spoke this Awakening Dhāraṇī amidst the great assembly, saying:
Oṃ sarvatathāgatamanyasatani padme jvala jvala dharmadhātu-garbhe manye manye mahāmanyetathāgata-hṛdaye manye svāhā. Having spoken this Great Illuminating Awakening Dhāraṇī, he concluded.
The mountains, forests, and great earth shook in six ways.
All Tathāgatas praised him with one voice, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, Tathāgata Śākyamuni!"
Having well expounded this most supreme secret dhāraṇī,
a cloud of Jambū-river gold appeared in the sky,
pervading the ten directions.
From within those clouds, a rain of the seven precious gems fell;
furthermore, a rain of nāgagandha sandalwood powder fell,
and a rain of udumbara flowers fell.
And with these, as well as various other exquisite flowers,
they further rained down lotuses, kumudas, and puṇḍarīkas.
Sūvarṇadīpa flowers,
māndārava flowers, mahāmāndārava flowers,
roca flowers, and mahāroca flowers.
With *mañjūṣaka* flowers, great *mañjūṣaka* flowers,
*sumana* flowers, *mallikā* flowers, and *campaka* flowers, they made offerings to the Buddha. Thereupon,
blazing fires broke out in all the palaces of Māra.
All the hosts of Māras were despondent and withered with grief, struck with great terror;
all the obstructors and Vināyakas were seized with alarm and fear,
their bodies covered in sweat, emitting foul odors as they fled in all ten directions.
All the devas who have conceived pure faith within the Buddha's teaching,
as well as the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth.
Each holding offering implements, they reverently made offerings to the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, there was the Bodhisattva Maṇiprabhāsasamudgata as their leader,
together with immeasurable koṭī-nayuta-hundreds-of-thousands of bodhisattvas.
They all made offerings to the Buddha with various kinds of exquisite jewels.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi was the leader,
together with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of vidyādhara ṛṣis.
Each held various hundreds of thousands of celestial garments to make offerings to the Buddha.
Furthermore, there were the Four Great Heavenly Kings,
together with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of hosts of the Four Heavenly Kings.
They made offerings to the Buddha with various kinds of incense, flowers, ointments, powdered incense, flower garlands, robes, banners, and canopies.
Furthermore, Brahmā and the various devas of the Brahma realm came to make offerings as well.
Furthermore, there were the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven together with hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of devaputras,
with Śakra as their leader, making offerings to the Buddha;
likewise, there were Nārāyaṇas and Maheśvaras.
Ratnabhadra, Pūrṇabhadra, Devaśakti, and others likewise came to make offerings.
Furthermore, the Sun and Moon Devas were in the sky,
making offerings to the Buddha.
Furthermore, there were the goddess Mahāśrī, the goddess Mahāprajñā,
the goddess Śaṅkhinī, and the yakṣiṇī Hārītī,
accompanied by a retinue of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of yakṣas.
Furthermore, there were the great goddess Vimalā, the goddess Vajrakālī,
the goddess Puṣpadantī, and the messenger goddess Mahādevī;
each of these hundreds of thousands of millions offered celestial palaces to the Buddha as an act of worship.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable hosts of gandharvas who performed hundreds of thousands of kinds of celestial,
exquisite music as an offering to the Buddha.
Additionally, there was an assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nāga kings.
Namely, the Nāga King Sāgara, the Nāga King Nanda, the Nāga King Upananda,
the Nāga King Vāruṇa, the Nāga King Supratiṣṭhita, the Nāga King Ratnaśikhin, and the Nāga King Samantavyūhaparipūrṇavigraha.
They made offerings to the Buddha with various kinds of radiant, flavorful jewels.

Furthermore, there was a wheel-turning monarch accompanied by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of ministers, palace attendants, and court ladies, as well as a thousand [sons].
The sons surrounded him and came to make offerings to the Buddha.
At that time, the great earth transformed into vajra,
and from before the Tathāgata, seven-jeweled lotus flowers surged forth from the ground.
Its flower has a hundred petals.
Within that flower is a Jambūnada-vajra thousand-spoked precious wheel,
its radiance brilliant and blazing like the sun.
That light shone universally throughout the trichiliocosm.
From within the circle of his navel, a subtle and wondrous sound issued forth,
speaking these words:
Excellent, excellent, Śākyamuni Tathāgata!
You are able to proclaim such secret dhāraṇīs,
able to turn the unsurpassed Great Wheel of Dharma, and able to proceed to the site of great enlightenment.
This dhāraṇī is the secret heart-vidyā of all Tathāgatas;
it is the heart-vidyā of the true principle of all Tathāgatas.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will further explain this Great Jewel Vast Pavilion Dhāraṇī.
The Blessed One has already spoken the *cittāloka-dhāraṇī*.
By means of this dhāraṇī,
all Tathāgatas together with their assemblies are awakened.
All have gathered for this assembly.
World-Honored One, now is the very time for you to speak this secret dhāraṇī.
World-Honored One, this dhāraṇī is the root of attaining Buddhahood.
It can eliminate all transgressions and exhaust the ocean of all suffering;
it can obstruct and halt the vast wilderness of all birth and death,
and enable one to cross over the torrential flood of all afflictions.
Without this dhāraṇī, the Great Vidyārājñī,
one can never achieve unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment;
this dhāraṇī is the seed for attaining Buddhahood.
This is the turning of the great wheel of Dharma;
this is the kindling of the great torch of Dharma;
this is the erecting of the great banner of Dharma; this is the blowing of the great conch of Dharma.
This is the Great Dharma Drum, the lion throne of the Dharma Master.
Excellent, World-Honored One! We pray that you will extensively explain for the great assembly this Great Dhāraṇī King, the methods for the maṇḍala, the mudrās, and the painted images.
At that time, a great assembly gathered like clouds:
devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others,
all of whom gave rise to a sense of rare and extraordinary wonder.
They all paid homage to the World-Honored One and stood gazing up at him.
At that time, having heard the great assembly’s sincere request,
the World-Honored One immediately expounded for them in detail this Dharma of the Great King of Teachings, the Dhāraṇī.
Chapter Two: The Fundamental Dhāraṇī. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly:
"I shall now proclaim this King of Dhāraṇī Teachings."
This dhāraṇī can bring about the accomplishment of unsurpassed bodhi.
If there are those who receive and uphold it, it can eliminate all karmic offenses of sin.
When the body attains purity, one then recites the root dhāraṇī, which says:

*Namo sarvatathāgatebhyaḥ oṃ vibhūṣaṇe maṇiprabhe tathatā nirdoṣiṇi maṇi maṇi suprabhe vimale sākṣare gābhihre hūṃ hūṃ jvala jvala buddhavilokite guhyādhiṣṭhitabhūṣaṇe svāhā.* At that time, the World-Honored One had finished speaking this Great Jewel Vast Pavilion Well-Established Secret Root Dhāraṇī.
The great earth shook in six ways,
raining down a great rain of jewels and magnificent flowers;
the entire assembled multitude rejoiced and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
It enables all wholesome dharmas to be fully accomplished and the attainment of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
At that time, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions praised the Tathāgata Śākyamuni with one voice, saying:
Excellent, Śākyamuni Tathāgata!
You are indeed able to proclaim this dharani for entering the bodhimanda.
Should one merely hear this dharani...
It eliminates all evil destinies;
merely by recollecting this dhāraṇī,
one is as if offering various exquisite flowers, unguents, powdered incense, and aromatic powders.
One makes offerings to all Buddhas of the ten directions;
if one can recite it even once, one will immediately attain non-retrogression from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment,
even after hundreds, thousands, or hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
All Tathāgatas cannot fully praise its efficacy;
this dhāraṇī possesses great majestic power,
and no māras whatsoever can ever create obstacles for it.
No enemies, wicked companions, ghosts, spirits, yakṣas, rākṣasas, humans, or non-humans shall find an opportunity against them;
they will increase immeasurable roots of goodness.
If one merely recites this dhāraṇī, [this shall come to pass].
The merit obtained is immeasurable; how much more so for one who is able to recite and uphold it for a long time—their merit cannot be calculated.
At that time, the yakṣa general Vajrapāṇi...
Together with the Four Great Heavenly Kings,
they went to where the Buddha was, joined their palms in reverence,
prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and stood there making offerings.
They addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, we shall protect all sentient beings who uphold this dhāraṇī;
through our empowerment and nurturing, we shall cause them all to rejoice.
At that time, the World-Honored One extended his golden hand.
He placed his hand upon the crown of the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi and comforted the four Great Heavenly Kings,
speaking these words:
I entrust this dhāraṇī to you.
Should there be anyone who upholds this dhāraṇī,
you must provide protection for them.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi and the Four Great Heavenly Kings addressed the Buddha,
saying: "World-Honored One, having received this entrustment,
we shall [uphold] this great King of Teachings."
One should always protect those sentient beings who uphold this dhāraṇī.
Chapter Three: The Heart and Auxiliary Dhāraṇīs. At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke the Heart Dhāraṇī, saying:
Oṃ maṇivajre hūṃ. At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke this heart-mantra (*hṛdaya-dhāraṇī*):
Oṃ maṇinidhe hūṃ phaṭ. If one recites and maintains this root mantra, [the following shall occur].
Without needing to select specific dates, times, lunar mansions, or planets,
and without being restricted by fasting or ritual observances,
one need only recite it ten thousand times in full.
Thereafter, before the Buddha or before a stupa containing his relics,
on the fifteenth day of the waxing moon,
one should bathe and purify oneself, and put on fresh, clean garments.
According to one's capacity, make offerings by lighting four lamps and scattering various incenses and flowers.
One who upholds this dhāraṇī should partake of the three white foods and circumambulate the caitya one hundred and eight times.
Recite the dhāraṇī one hundred and eight times,
then rest and sleep in that very place.
When dawn is about to break, the Tathāgata will immediately manifest his body before you.
The Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi also appears before them.
All their aspirations shall be fulfilled as they wish.
Even those who have committed the five crimes of immediate retribution [shall attain this].
Perform this rite for a third time;
only then will you be able to evoke the manifestation. Do not give rise to doubt or uncertainty.
Constantly recite it one hundred and eight times at the clear dawn.
All that one seeks shall be accomplished;
no malevolent charms or various poisons shall be able to cause harm,
nor can water sweep one away.
Fire cannot burn them;
thieves cannot plunder them; illness cannot invade them.
They have no fear of external enemies and are always free from serious illness.
Furthermore, there shall be no diseases of the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, mouth, teeth, or lips; nor shall there be headaches or pains in the neck and joints;
nor shall there be fevers that recur every day, every second day, every third day, or every fourth day.
None of these will adhere to their bodies.
No evil venomous snakes, tigers, wolves, birds, or beasts can cause them harm.
Even curses, incantations, and spells shall not affect them.
Such is the power of this dhāraṇī:
it can pacify all fears, extinguish all evil obstacles,
generate all merits, and bring the six pāramitās to fulfillment.
One will be able to accomplish the realm of the Tathāgata.
Merely by reciting this dhāraṇī,
all undertakings can be successfully accomplished.
If there is anyone who ascends to the summit of a great high mountain and recites this dhāraṇī,
all sentient beings within the range of their vision shall have all their karmic offenses extinguished.
Furthermore, one will be freed from all karma leading to the hells and escape all rebirths among the animals.
If one enters a temple of the gods and recites this dhāraṇī,
it shall cause all the celestial deities to respectfully obey its instructions.
If one enters a dragon pool and recites this dhāraṇī, all the hosts of dragons will come to take refuge in them.
If one recites this dhāraṇī before the sun rises, [the same shall occur].
The Sun Deity will immediately appear before that person and fulfill all their wishes and aspirations. Furthermore,
if anyone recites this dhāraṇī in the presence of the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, [their desires shall likewise be granted].
The Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi will appear before them, and whatever they seek or wish for shall be granted according to their desire.
Furthermore, if anyone takes the root of achyranthes (kanghui) and recites this dhāraṇī, [their wishes shall likewise be fulfilled].
If one recites it one thousand and eight times while holding it in the mouth,
then whatever is spoken within the royal palace will cause the queens,
consorts, and maidservants to rejoice with pure faith.
If one consecrates black pepper and holds it in the mouth,
all the words spoken when conversing with others will be received with faith and they shall give rise to joy.
If one consecrates white mustard seeds one thousand and eight times and casts them into the air, [the same result follows].
All evil winds, thunder, and hail will be completely dispersed.
If one consecrates salt one hundred and eight times,
pure-practicing Brahmins will all come to revere and love him.
Those who eat this salt shall all attain joy.

If one wishes to cause a kṣatriya to feel respect and affection, one should take white mustard seeds and perform a homa of one thousand and eight repetitions; then one will immediately attain their respect and affection.
If one consecrates agallochum incense one thousand and eight times and burns it before any patient afflicted by ghosts or demons,
they will all speak according to their own wishes.
That illness will be cured immediately.
If there is a severe drought, first smear the ground with cow dung and construct a square altar measuring four cubits on each side.
In the center, draw a single pool,
two cubits square and colored blue.
Within the pool, take *gomaya* mixed with earth to form clay, and mold it into the shape of a nāga.
From the waist upward, it takes the form of a bodhisattva body with the face of a bodhisattva;
from its head, three snake heads emerge.
From the waist downward, he has the body of a serpent,
coiled within the pond;
his entire body is smeared with yellow cinnabar, making it appear red.
Adhere gold leaf to the heart of the dragon.
Surround the four sides of the altar with lotus flowers drawn in white powder.
Insert four arrows at the four corners of the maṇḍala and encircle the maṇḍala with five-colored threads wound around those arrows.
Furthermore, suspend small five-colored banners along the lines.
Place four water jars at the four corners and set incense burners at the four gates.
Furthermore, use four small flasks:
one flask filled with milk,
and one flask filled with curd.
One vessel is filled with milk-rice and another with clarified butter,
along with granulated sugar; furthermore,
four lamps are lit and four kinds of incense are burned.

That is to say, one should scatter on the altar seven kinds of grains—barley, wheat, rice, mung beans, sesame, mustard seeds, and white mustard seeds—as well as frankincense, *donglu*, white sandalwood, and *suhexiang*. One should also offer five-colored foods and drinks along with various flowers and fruits, while the practitioner sits facing east to perform the recitation.
First, take white mustard seeds and recite the dhāraṇī over them one thousand and eight times;
after this empowerment, take a single white mustard seed.
Recite the dhāraṇī once and nail it onto the head of the dragon;
when one thousand and eight recitations are completed,
that dragon will immediately send down rain.
All nāgas are subdued.
If one wishes to stop rain, empower white mustard seeds one hundred and eight times and cast them into the dragon pool;
the rain will immediately cease.
If there is evil wind, hail, or rain,
take *khadira* wood and fashion stakes;
by nailing them into the edge of a dragon pond, frost and hail will cease to fall and the evil winds will immediately stop.
If one wishes to bind a vināyaka,
take white mustard seeds and empower them one hundred and eight times;
then place them upon the head of the vināyaka.
Thus, they will be unable to create obstacles.
By washing the Vināyakas with milk, one immediately attains liberation;
all undertakings will then be successfully accomplished.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Daxingshan Monastery, who was the Duke of Sū, with a fief of three thousand households, invested with purple robes, posthumously honored as Minister of Works, and bestowed the title Dàjiàn (Great Mirror) and the epithet Dàguǎngzhì (Great Universal Wisdom). Chapter Four: The Method for Accomplishing the Citta-dhāraṇī. In general, for one who performs the rites for accomplishing the Citta-dhāraṇī, if they recite it one hundred thousand times, they shall immediately behold all the Tathāgatas.
By reciting it two hundred thousand times, one shall behold all buddha-fields.
By reciting it three hundred thousand times, one shall attain entry into all maṇḍalas,
and all mantra-dharmas will be fully accomplished.
By reciting four hundred thousand times, one becomes a Wheel-Turning King among the Vidyādharas.
By reciting five hundred thousand times, the gates of all the asuras, the hermitages of the ṛṣis,
and the palaces of the nāgas shall open of their own accord, and one will gain entry to them all.
If one recites it six hundred thousand times, one will behold all hidden treasures (*nidhi*).
If one recites it seven hundred thousand times, one will immediately remember and know the events of one's past lives throughout immeasurable births.
If one recites it eight hundred thousand times, one immediately attains the *ratnamudrā-samādhi*.
If one recites it nine hundred thousand times, one attains the empowerment of the playful supernatural powers (*vikrīḍita-ṛddhi*) of all bodhisattvas.
If one recites it one million times, one will receive the empowerment of all Tathāgatas and assemble together with all Tathāgatas.
Thus, merit and wisdom will increase manifold, and one will attain immeasurable, supreme qualities.
If one has committed the five crimes of immediate retribution,
slandered the noble ones, or slandered the true Dharma,
such that one ought to enter the Avīci Hell;
By reciting this dhāraṇī one hundred thousand times,
all karmic obstructions will be completely extinguished;
one will attain non-retrogression and acquire the wisdom of recollecting past lives.
All Tathāgatas protect, mindfully attend to, and embrace them.
They attain purity of the eye, purity of the ear, purity of the nose,
purity of the tongue, and purity of the body.
One increases immeasurable and supreme meritorious qualities;
one undergoes a transformation to receive a body and karma that are increasingly pure,
while simultaneously attaining the successful accomplishment of various worldly undertakings according to one's wishes.
Furthermore, the method for realgar is explained:
take high-quality realgar and place it in a vessel of refined copper.
Beginning from the thirteenth day of the waxing moon, [one should proceed].
Having bathed cleanly and put on fresh, pure garments,
one should consume the "three white foods"— namely, milk, curd, and non-glutinous rice—
and perform one hundred thousand recitations of empowerment before the Buddha.
On the night of the fifteenth day,
the consecrated realgar will manifest three signs of accomplishment:
if it becomes warm, emits smoke, or blazes with flames, then accomplishment is attained.
If one uses the "warm" [substance] to dot the forehead,
one immediately attains the accomplishment of *antaḥpura* (entry into the inner palace) and gains access to the caves of the Asuras, as well as all the palaces of the ṛṣis and nāgas.
One will attain the rank of a Vidyādhara Cakravartin,
and all that one intends to do will be accomplished.
If smoke issues forth, use it to apply as an ointment to the eyes.
One shall see all the palatial abodes of the bodhisattvas,
as well as all the bodhisattvas of the Vajra family;
no evil māras whatsoever shall be able to create obstacles.
One attains the treasury of all dharmas;
wherever one goes, one achieves thorough penetration.
If one manifests blazing light, one immediately soars into the void.
One attains the *dīpa-pradīpa-dhāraṇī-samādhi* and becomes a sovereign among the Trāyastriṃśa gods,
obtaining all that is required.
If one recites it ten thousand times atop a mountain peak, one will be respected by all sentient beings;
whatever is sought shall be attained, and all people of Jambudvīpa will come to pay homage.
If one enters a body of water and recites [the mantra] one thousand and eight times,
all nāgas will be completely subdued.
Take white mustard seeds and empower them by reciting [the mantra] one thousand and eight times.
If one scatters [the mantra] into the void, rain will fall at that very moment, subduing all nāgas.
If one constantly recites and maintains it day after day, one will obtain great auspiciousness.
If one suffers from any illness whatsoever...
Take one bottle of water and add one part each of the following: the drug Indrāhastikā (white *arka*), the drug Prakṣa (red *arka*), white mustard seeds, saffron, and white sandalwood.
Place it inside a flask and empower it one thousand times.
By sprinkling this scented water upon the crown of the head,
all those suffering from severe and chronic illnesses shall be completely cured.
Furthermore, all karmic obstacles and transgressions will be extinguished;
all talismans, incantations, and suppressive rites shall be entirely eradicated,
and one will obtain all manner of supreme auspiciousness.
If one suffers from leprosy,
bathing and performing the consecration will also bring about recovery.
If one suffers from vitiligo, [the same applies].
By sprinkling water upon the crown of the head, one may also achieve recovery from illness.
If there is a woman who desires a son,
by sprinkling water upon her crown of the head, she shall immediately give birth to a son.
If there is anyone who has long maintained the recitation but finds no spiritual efficacy or *siddhi*, and does not see the deity before them,
by performing this initiation rite (*abhiṣeka*), they will swiftly attain *siddhi*.
Such are the mundane and supramundane [attainments].
All sought-after wishes shall be fully accomplished.
Chapter Five: The Ritual for Accomplishing the *Sūci-manas* Dhāraṇī. Recite the *Sūci-manas* Dhāraṇī ten thousand times.
All the spirits and deities who create obstacles and difficulties all came to prostrate at his feet and said:
"O Vidyādhara, protect us; do not take our lives."
Whatever I am commanded to do, I shall certainly accomplish;
I shall achieve it all.
If one recites this twenty-one thousand times, [the goal will be attained].
One will immediately attain the reverence and submission of all devas and nāgas, becoming a sovereign among the gods;
whatever words one utters, the devas shall all carry out.
If one recites it thirty thousand times, [the same result shall be achieved].
All spirits, yakṣas, and the like will all submit and be subdued.
If one recites it forty thousand times,
the summoning of those one desires will be accomplished at will.
If one recites it fifty thousand times,
one will be able to summon and capture whoever one desires— whether gods, nāgas, yakṣas, or gandharvas.
Whether they be kinnaras, asuras, mahoragas, and the retinues of rishis, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas;
or kṣatriya kings, queens, ministers, and court officials.
Furthermore, all other various types of persons shall obtain their wishes.
By burning guggulu incense mixed with white mustard seeds and reciting [the mantra] sixty thousand times, one attains the stainless samādhi.

If one recites it seventy thousand times, one will become a Wheel-Turning King among the Vidyādharas; if one recites it eighty thousand times, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi together with his retinue will appear before one.
If one recites it ninety thousand times, all bodhisattvas will grant one fearlessness.
If one recites it one hundred thousand times, one shall behold all the Tathāgatas,
and those Tathāgatas will speak these words:
"Son of good family, you shall go to all the Buddha-fields wherever you desire,
attaining mastery without obstruction;
you shall penetrate all mantras and penetrate all sutras and treatises."
Sustained by the empowerment of all Tathāgatas,
they shall never regress from *samyak-saṃbodhi* and shall attain various mundane and supramundane dharmas.
Whatever the mind delights in seeking shall all be accomplished.
All Buddhas and Tathāgatas shall grant their seal of approval.
Chapter Six: The Dhāraṇīs of Various Rituals. Regarding the Mantra for Sitting:
Oṃ maṇi-kuṇḍali hūṃ hūṃ svāhā. Recite this seven times, and then sit down to perform the remaining protective rites.
Next, the mantra for binding the boundaries of the maṇḍala is as follows:
Oṃ maṇivijaye dhara dhara hūṃ svāhā. Recite this mantra seven times over white mustard seeds and scatter them in the four directions;
thus, the boundary is established.
Next, the mantra for binding the boundaries of the ten directions is as follows:
Oṃ jvalitamaṇi-locana hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. Recite this mantra to consecrate the scented water.
Recite the mantra over white mustard seeds one hundred and eight times;
scattering them throughout the ten directions constitutes the binding of the boundaries of the ten directions.
The mantra for expelling the Vināyakas is as follows:
Oṃ maṇi-prabhavati hara hara hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. Recite this mantra.
Consecrate the ash-water twenty-one times and scatter it in the ten directions.
The Uṣṇīṣa mantra is as follows:
Oṃ vajramaṇi tiṣṭha tiṣṭha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. Recite this mantra seven times to perform the consecration.
Form a fist with the right hand and extend the thumb;
rub it over the crown of the head three times in a clockwise direction,
and one’s body will immediately be protected.
The mantra for consecrating the robe is:
Oṃ maṇiviśuddhe dṛdhi dṛdhi hūṃ phaṭ. Recite this mantra seven times to consecrate the clothing.
The mantra for washing and rinsing is:
Oṃ vinyurbodhi hara hara mahāmani hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. Recite this mantra to empower the water for washing the hands and rinsing the mouth.
And by using it to sprinkle upon the body,
one can purify the sense faculties.
The mantra for bathing is as follows:
Oṃ sunirmalavati hara hara sphoṭaya sphoṭaya mri mri hūṃ svāhā. Recite this mantra one hundred and eight times over white mustard seeds and water to empower them for the ritual of bathing the body.
The protection mantra is:
Oṃ maṇidhari hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ (with a short vowel). Recite this mantra and sprinkle it upon all incense, flowers, fruits, food, drink, and all other articles to be used.
All are to be consecrated and protected by means of this mantra.
The mantra for the divine cord (*śūla-sūtra*) is:
Oṃ dṛḍhe dṛḍhe vimalakari hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. The mantra for the offering is:
Oṃ sarvatathāgatapūjāmaṇi hūṃ hūṃ. Recite this mantra to consecrate all flowers;
recite it also at the time of scattering them.
The mantra for scented ointment is as follows:
Oṃ sarvatathāgatagandhamani-spharaṇa hūṃ. This is the mantra for incense.
Oṃ jvalitamaṇi-aparājita-spharaṇa vidhi hūṃ. This is the mantra for the lamp.
Oṃ jvalitārcire dāvāli hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. The mantra for offering food is:
Oṃ pravaravāra-vati sara sara hūṃ hūṃ. The mantra for offering arghya is: [as above].
Oṃ mahāmanibhūṣaye dhara dhara hūṃ hūṃ. This is the mantra for offering the articles of worship, food, and so forth.
Oṃ mahāvimale hūṃ hūṃ vara vara hūṃ. This is the homa mantra.
Oṃ jvala-sphura-gagana-prataraṇi hūṃ hūṃ. This is the mantra for consecrating the rosary.
Oṃ luñjiramani pramardaya hūṃ. With this mantra, empower the rosary seven times.
Then recite the root mantra.
Each time one moves a single bead,
it constitutes reciting the mantras spoken by all Tathāgatas once; thus,
each and every mantra becomes recited immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of times.
The mantra for recitation is as follows: When one wishes to recite the root mantra, one should first recite this mantra:
Oṃ vajramanikara kiṃkari hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ (with a half-syllable). The mantra for sitting in the full-lotus posture (*paryaṅka*) is as follows:
Oṃ subhāvitavijaye mani mani svāhā. This is the mantra for awakening all Tathāgatas.
Oṃ sarvatathāgatavajrābhyudgataratna hūṃ maṇikaraṇe svāhā. This is the mantra for inviting all the Tathāgatas.
Oṃ vibhūrapravāre duru duru hūṃ hūṃ. The mantra for making requests is:
Oṃ sarvatathāgatādhiṣṭhānajñānasamrakṣaṇavajre hūṃ hūṃ. The mantra for requesting the bodhisattva’s vows is:
Oṃ subrahmaṇye hana hana hūṃ. This is the mantra for summoning all devas and nāgas.
Oṃ abhiṣamaye vārī dhara dhara hūṃ. This is the mantra for summoning the Four Great Kings and others.
Oṃ maṇivigavati hūṃ. This is the mantra for empowering the disciple.
Oṃ śubhamani hulu hulu hūṃ. This is the mantra for empowering the disciple and causing the disciple to enter the maṇḍala.
Oṃ sarvatathāgatahr̥dayavajriṇi dharadharā hūṃ hūṃ. This is the mantra for offering food to all Buddhas, all Bodhisattvas, and the various devas.
Oṃ vīra vīra śigagaṇa vahini lahu lahu hūṃ hūṃ. All incense, flowers, food, and drink should be offered while reciting this mantra.
The mantra for protecting the body is:
Oṃ maṇi-sūm-bhaṇi-vijayavati-ṛkṣa-ṛkṣa-maṃ hūṃ. The mantra for dismissing the assembly of noble ones is as follows:
Oṃ sarvatathāgatagulodadhisamara vigati jvala jvala hūṃ hūṃ svāhā. Recite this mantra for use in all circumstances.
This refers to the offerings of the principal deity, such as argha water, incense, flowers, food,
and other requisites. For all of the above heart-mantras,
one should first recite each one one hundred and eight times.
Then, when performing the ritual,
as soon as one recites [the mantra] that extinguishes all sins,
one shall attain liberation from all suffering and affliction.
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, will certainly bestow upon them the prophecy of enlightenment;
they shall surely attain Buddhahood.
All evil karma from previous lives shall be entirely dispelled through the upholding of this mantra.
They shall attain immeasurable merits equal in number to the sands of the Ganges,
swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
and be able to turn the wheel of Dharma.
Chapter Seven: Establishing the Maṇḍala. At that time, the Blessed One taught the ritual procedures for the maṇḍala.
According to the proper time and the Dharma, one should first select an excellent site.
Thereafter, one constructs an altar.
The altar shall be four cubits in size with four gates;
it should be smeared all over with a mixture of cow dung and earth.
Spread a white canopy over the altar,
matching its dimensions;
from the center of the altar, measure out two cubits.
Construct a small square altar.
First, smear it with white sandalwood incense;
next, apply saffron to it.
One may either roll it from five-colored powders or draw it;
use colored pigments within a new vessel for this purpose.
Within a small mandala, draw a pavilion made of the seven treasures.
Inside the pavilion, draw the image of a single Buddha in the posture of preaching the Dharma.
Before the Buddha, he fashioned a lotus flower adorned with the seven precious gems;
within the calyx of the lotus, he painted a wheel.
Its wheel has a hundred spokes, complete with a rim,
and is adorned with gold;
outside the wheel, flames are painted.
The stem of that lotus is the color of vaidūrya.
To the left of the Buddha, one should paint the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi in a wrathful form.
The right hand holds a vajra and the left hand holds a white fly-whisk.
To the right, paint the Bodhisattva Maṇivajra,
his body adorned with various kinds of necklaces and ornaments.
The left hand holds a jewel, and the right hand holds a white fly-whisk.
In each of the four corners, one of the Four Great Heavenly Kings is depicted,
wearing armor and holding weapons in their hands.
His body is adorned with various crowns and necklaces;
he assumes a wrathful form.
Within the small mandala, one should draw a boundary path of the seven treasures.
Suspend a single parasol above the center of the maṇḍala,
measuring one cubit in size,
and hang banners all around its four sides.
At the eastern gate of the great maṇḍala, hang silk banners of five colors.
Fill four golden vases with scented water,
and within the vases place the seven precious gems, various fragrant medicines, and the five grains.
Insert flowering branches and fruit-bearing twigs into the mouths of the vases,
tie silk cloths around the necks of the vases,
and place them at the four corners of the altar.
Furthermore, fill four silver vases with milk and place them at the four corners of the great mandala;
if silver vases are unavailable, [use gold ones].
Replace them with vases made of gold and silver.
Within the southern gate of the central altar,
depict the Great Auspicious Goddess (Mahāśrīdevī).
Her body is adorned with various kinds of necklaces and ornaments.
In the center of the northern gate, one should paint the goddess Śaṅkhinī;
in the center of the western gate of the maṇḍala, one should paint the goddess Vajradūtī.
With eight arms holding various weapons and adorned with diverse necklaces and ornaments,
a blue silk banner is suspended above.
Within the four sides of the central altar,
offer incense, flowers, food, and drink according to one's means,
and light thirty-two lamps.
Scatter various kinds of flowers and fruits upon the altar.
Place a golden incense burner before the Buddha image and burn aloeswood incense.
Before the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, one burns agallochum incense in a silver incense burner;
before the Bodhisattva Maṇivajra, one likewise burns blended incense with clarified butter in a silver incense burner.
Before the Four Heavenly Kings, burn incense of *kunkuma* (guggulu) mixed with *śrī-gandha* (white resin).
Before the goddess Śrī-devī, burn white altar-incense (*śveta-maṇḍala-dhūpa*).
Before the goddess Śāṅkhinī, burn *guggula* incense.
One should burn sāragandha incense— which is resinous incense— before the Vajra female messengers,
and offer various foods and drinks individually before each of the Four Great Kings and the others.
Outside each of the four gates of the central maṇḍala,
auspicious banners are erected.
In the center of the eastern gate of the great maṇḍala, Hārītī is depicted.
Surrounded by his seven sons,
Mahādeva, the Heavenly King, is to be painted within the southern gate;
Puṣpadantī, the Rākṣasī, is to be painted within the western gate.
In the northern gate, paint the goddess Bhīmā,
beautiful of countenance and surrounded by seven female attendants.
On the four sides of the maṇḍala, insert thirty-two arrows.
Each individual arrow is encircled on all sides by threads empowered with the five colors;
small banners of the five colors are suspended from these threads as ornaments.
Outside the great maṇḍala, upon the path of the food boundary,
one should arrange various flowers, various flavors of food and drink, various fruits, seven kinds of oil cakes, thirty-two trays, thirty-two vases, and thirty-two incense burners.
Light one hundred and eight oil lamps.

Burn various powdered incenses and various burning incenses, namely: *kunkuma*, *guggulu*, *bhallātaka*, *mūṣaka*, white sandalwood, aloeswood, *tāmarasa*, *sahakāra*, *sāragha*, and *nīlaguḍa*. One should also burn five kinds of honey-fragrance incense.
Furthermore, one should use camphor, musk, saffron, red sandalwood, white sandalwood, and so forth,
each as an unguent. Next,
one should offer food and drink, such as milk, curd, sugar-water, stone honey, and water.
Place eight jars [of water] in each [vessel],
and eight bowls of milk gruel.
Furthermore, prepare eight bowls of gruel made by mixing non-glutinous rice, mung beans, and sesame seeds.
There were eight bowls each of non-glutinous rice and *modaka* cakes;
